verdicts.REASON: A section heading. It asserts no factual state about the world, a person or the source; connective/rhetorical framing only.

The attribution is only that what follows is the account the review gives. The review does give such an account: 'But EAF is also a big, unwieldy, confusing thing' and 'You've just got to follow your nose and hope you sniff out something you like.' Nothing is attributed to the reviewer that the review does not carry.

A reading of grounded material: 'big, unwieldy, confusing', 'impossible to figure out how any of it fits together', 'follow your nose'. Moving-through-rather-than-reading is the article's synthesis of those, and smuggles in no name, date, number or new factual state.
Verbatim: 'There are curated displays, satellite exhibitions, performances, off-site projects'.
Directly stated by the source: 'it's impossible to figure out how any of it fits together'.
A metaphorical restatement of 'impossible to figure out how any of it fits together'. It does not assert that a festival map exists or was consulted; no new concrete fact.

The review does state this plainly and in its own voice as the way to proceed: 'You've just got to follow your nose and hope you sniff out something you like.' The predicate attributed (a plainly stated method) is exactly what the sentence does.
The asserted state is stated in the source itself: 'hope you sniff out something you like'.
Terrain-not-argument is an evaluative characterisation of a grounded method ('follow your nose', 'impossible to figure out how any of it fits together'). Adds no factual state.

Metaphor extending the terrain figure, drawing on the grounded consistency the review reports ('the whole festival is a celebration of the underground and unheralded', 'You can't walk into a gallery without...'). No new concrete fact; empty anchor is not disqualifying for SUBJECT_MATTER.
The review does say the claim that follows: 'You can't walk into a gallery without learning about some subcultural genius or longlost creative you've never heard of.'
Near-verbatim reproduction of the source sentence, correctly attributed to the review.
The visitor's state of prior ignorance is stated in the source: 'some subcultural genius or longlost creative you've never heard of'.
The article drawing out what the grounded 'you can't walk into a gallery without...' implies across the festival. No new fact.
'Room after room' restates the source's every-gallery claim in the article's own figure. It asserts no specific count of rooms or names.

Extraction returned no anchor, but the source has one: 'some subcultural genius or longlost creative you've never heard of'. Never having heard of the name entails not possessing it at any earlier moment, so the asserted prior state is licensed; 'an hour earlier' marks recency, not an independent duration fact about the visit.
An editorial judgement about which material to set down, echoing the source's own 'is worth telling'. Evaluative, not factual.
The review does note these facts: 'She was a black photographer and photojournalist who documented life on the margins of inner city Edinburgh.'
Verbatim: 'She was a black photographer and photojournalist'.
Verbatim: 'who documented life on the margins of inner city Edinburgh'.
The review makes exactly this comparison: 'Like a lot of people in EAF, she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime'.
Verbatim: 'she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime'.
Verbatim, date included: 'was only discovered after her death in 2013'.
Verbatim: 'Frank Walter (1926-2009), an Antiguan painter, writer, poet and polymath'.
'The group show at Ingleby Gallery... It's all centred on Frank Walter' licenses both the venue and the centring.
Verbatim: 'who died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime'.
The quantity is the source's own: 'the thousands of paintings and drawings'.
Correct provenance claim: the figure 'thousands' appears in the review itself, not imported by the article.

A negative claim about the source, and it is borne out by reading the whole source: 'thousands' occurs once, inside a subordinate clause, and nothing anywhere in the review remarks on the quantity (the surrounding comment is about the work being 'small, subtle, strange').
The reviewer states a first-person position on hidden stories: 'I think they have a duty - to viewers and to their subjects - to tell them clearly.'
The review does argue the position that follows; same anchor sentence.
Near-verbatim reproduction of the source's conditional duty claim, correctly marked as the review's.
Verbatim: 'to viewers and to their subjects - to tell them clearly'.
The specific thing attributed - that the demand concerns the telling - is what the anchor says: the duty is 'to tell them clearly'.
Two parties are named in the source clause: viewers and subjects. A checkable count against the anchor, and it checks out.
'to viewers' is named in the anchor.
'to their subjects' is named in the anchor.
A paraphrase of a single conjoined duty owed to two named parties; 'both directions at once' adds no factual state beyond the anchor.
The article drawing out what the two-party duty implies. Causal form ('which means') is not itself evidence of anything; the causation is about the review's stated duty, which is grounded.
Restates the second limb of the grounded duty as a reading. No new fact about anyone.
Evaluative comparison between two obligations the source names. Comparative form is not by itself unsupported; the comparison is about the article's subject matter, not about a fact of the world.
Causal reading resting on grounded material - the artists in question are dead (George 1957-2013, Walter 1926-2009) and so cannot testify. No new concrete fact is smuggled.

The review does use a particular vocabulary for what happens in the galleries: 'you'll have uncovered so many hidden stories'. The claim attributes only specificity of word choice, which the anchor bears out.

A frequency claim about the source, checkable and true of the discovery vocabulary the article then lists: 'undiscovered archives', 'Another largely undiscovered artist', 'undiscovered narratives', plus 'was only discovered after her death' and 'sniff out'. Recurrence is established by the source itself.
'you'll have uncovered so many hidden stories' - the word is the review's.
'undiscovered archives' and 'Another largely undiscovered artist' - the word is the review's.
'hope you sniff out something you like' - the phrase is the review's; only the tense differs.
A claim about placement in the source, and it is correct: the Columbo sentence is the review's first sentence.
Verbatim from the opening sentence.
The asserted state is the source's own: 'you'll feel like Columbo'.

A gloss on the connotation of the review's chosen word, cued by the review's own detective figure ('you'll feel like Columbo') and by 'uncovered'. Characterising a word's register is not a factual state about the world, a person or the source's content.
The article's reading of what the second-person 'you'll have uncovered' does rhetorically. Analysis of grounded material, adding no new fact.
The review does so describe him: 'Another largely undiscovered artist, Sadao Hasegawa (1945-1999)'.
Verbatim, including the hedge 'largely', which the article preserves.
The framing attributed is the review's own wording: 'the whole festival is a celebration of the underground and unheralded'.
Verbatim reproduction, correctly marked as the review's framing.
The article's reading of the review's second-person discovery frame ('you'll have uncovered'). Sets up the later distinction; asserts no new fact.

'in August' is a specific time-fact about when the festival is walked, and the source text contains no month, date or season anywhere - it names only 'Edinburgh art festival' and 'EAF'. The extraction returned an empty anchor and none exists on a direct reading. An empty anchor cannot justify a CONCRETE_WORLD_DETAIL; the timing is imported from outside knowledge and stated as settled.

Characterises the tense and situation of the visitor's discovery as the review frames it ('By the time you're done... you'll have uncovered'; galleries you walk into). SUBJECT_MATTER carries no anchor obligation, and no name, date or number is added.
The article's central comparison, combining grounded facts about George and Walter. Legitimate even though the source never draws the comparison itself.
Verbatim: 'was only discovered after her death in 2013'.

Anchor: 'died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime'. 'Works he made' for 'paintings and drawings he amassed' is licensed in context - he is the painter whose work the show centres on.

The connotation attributed to the review's usage is carried by its own sentence - hidden stories surfacing and the detective's pleasure of the find ('you'll have uncovered so many hidden stories you'll feel like Columbo'), reinforced by 'a celebration of the underground and unheralded'. The article also frames it non-exclusively ('whatever the word carries').

Article-level reading built from two grounded facts: George 'was only discovered after her death in 2013' and Walter 'died having never shown any' of his work. The conclusion combines them; no new factual state is added.
That a finding occurred is directly licensed: 'was only discovered after her death in 2013'.
A metaphor for death, grounded in both artists' death dates and the posthumous discovery the source reports. The 'line' is figurative, not a new concrete fact.
The article conceding the validity of the review's sense of the word for the visitor. Evaluative, grounded in the review's second-person address.
A semantic claim about the scope of the word, not a negative claim about what the review says or omits. It rests on grounded facts about both artists' lifetimes.

Causal reading generalised across the two artists from 'she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime, and was only discovered after her death in 2013' and Walter's parallel case. Causal form is not itself evidence of anything, and no new fact is introduced.
Connective summation of the article's own distinction. Asserts nothing factual.

The sense of discovery the review deploys is addressed to the reader in the second person and located in the visit itself: 'By the time you're done with Edinburgh art festival you'll have uncovered so many hidden stories', and 'You can't walk into a gallery without learning about...'. Present and first-hand is what those sentences carry.
The anchor licenses both halves of the asserted state - the visitor learns about the artist and had 'never heard of' them beforehand.
Connective framing that sorts the article's own two senses. Asserts no new factual state.

Anchor licenses the specific claim: Walter 'died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime'; the source says the same of George, 'she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime'.
